## A Reminder About Our Goals

```{r}
set.seed(123)
num_pts <- 20 

x <- runif(num_pts, min = 0, max = 100)
y <- 7*x + 2 + rnorm(num_pts, mean = 0, sd = 100)

motivation_df <- tibble(
  x = x,
  y = y
)

mot_lr_spec <- linear_reg() 
mot_lr_rec <- recipe(y ~ x, data = motivation_df)
mot_lr_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(mot_lr_spec) %>%
  add_recipe(mot_lr_rec)

mot_lr_fit <- mot_lr_wf %>%
  fit(motivation_df)

plot_data <- tibble(
  x = seq(0, 100, length.out = 250),
)

plot_data <- mot_lr_fit %>%
  augment(plot_data) %>%
  bind_cols(
    mot_lr_fit %>%
      predict(plot_data, type = "conf_int") %>%
      rename(.conf_lower = .pred_lower,
             .conf_upper = .pred_upper)
  ) %>%
  bind_cols(
    mot_lr_fit %>%
      predict(plot_data, type = "pred_int")
  )

ggplot() + 
  geom_ribbon(data = plot_data,
              aes(x = x, ymin = .pred_lower, ymax = .pred_upper),
              fill = "grey",
              alpha = 0.3) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = plot_data,
              aes(x = x, ymin = .conf_lower, ymax = .conf_upper),
              fill = "grey",
              alpha = 0.6) + 
  geom_line(data = plot_data,
            aes(x = x, y = .pred),
            color = "blue",
            lwd = 2) +
  geom_point(data = motivation_df,
             aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  labs(title = "Let's Model y, given x", 
       x = "x",
       y = "y")
```

. . .

So...how do we do it?

## The Highlights {.smaller}

<div style="font-size:15pt">

:::{.fragment}

The approach we use will depend on the setting we find ourselves in: ***Statistical Learning*** (confirmatory/inferential) or ***Machine Learning*** (exploratory/predictive).

:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

**Statistical Learning:**

:::

+ Hypothesize a model form
+ Build a model using the `{tidymodels}` framework
  
  + Model specification (model class)
  + Recipe (defining the response, features, and transformations)
  + Workflow (pair specification and recipe)
  + Fit the workflow to the data

+ Assess model quality and fit

  + Global model metrics
  + Term-based assessments

+ Interpret the model

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

**Machine Learning:**

:::

+ Obtain training and validation data set(s)
+ EDA on training data
+ Build a model using the `{tidymodels}` framework
  
  + Model specification (model class)
  + Recipe (defining the response, features, and transformations)
  + Workflow (pair specification and recipe)
  + Fit the workflow to training data

+ Assess model performance

  + Global performance metrics (training data)
  + Compare predictive performance on training and validation data
  + We'll add more assessment techniques later

+ Iterate
+ Evaluate final model on test data and make new predictions

:::

::::

</div>

Each day we discuss regression models, we'll split time between modeling in the ***statistical learning*** and ***machine learning*** contexts.

:::

We'll use two separate data sets -- one for each context.

:::

:::{.fragment}

## Statistical Learning

<div style="font-size:18pt">

:::{.fragment}

In our *statistical learning* context, we come to the scenario with a hypothesis about the association between a response and available explanatory variable(s).

:::

:::{.fragment}

**The Objective:** We'll hypothesize and examine relationships between anatomical, physiological, spatial, and temporal variables with penguin body mass.

:::

:::{.fragment}

**1. Hypothesis:** Penguin body mass is associated with penguin flipper length.

:::

:::{.fragment}

**2. Hypothesized Model Form:** There are two forms in which we can write our models...

:::

:::{.fragment}

$$\text{body mass} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\cdot\left(\text{flipper length}\right) + \varepsilon$$

:::

:::{.fragment}

$$\mathbb{E}\left[\text{body mass}\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1\cdot\left(\text{flipper length}\right)$$

:::

:::{.fragment}

**3. Corresponding Hypothesis Test:** Just like in introductory statistics, we write a corresponding null (skeptical) hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis reflecting our original hypothesized relationship in item 1.

:::

:::{.fragment}

$$\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a & : & \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}$$

:::

</div>

## Statistical Learning

<div style="font-size:18pt">

**1. Hypothesis:** Penguin body mass is associated with penguin flipper length.

**2. Hypothesized Model Form:** $\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}\left[\text{body mass}\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1\cdot\left(\text{flipper length}\right)}$

**3. Corresponding Hypothesis Test:** $\displaystyle{\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a & : & \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}}$

:::{.fragment}

**4. Construct the Model:** We'll use the `{tidymodels}` framework to construct the model. It happens in four steps...(i) `specification`, (ii) `recipe`, (iii) `workflow`, and (iv) `fit`. 

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-2|4|6-8|10-12|"

lr_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

lr_rec <- recipe(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm, data = penguins)

lr_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lr_spec) |>
  add_recipe(lr_rec)

lr_fit <- lr_wf |>
  fit(penguins)
```

:::

</div>

<div style="font-size:18pt">

**1. Hypothesis:** Penguin body mass is associated with penguin flipper length.

**2. Hypothesized Model Form:** $\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}\left[\text{body mass}\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1\cdot\left(\text{flipper length}\right)}$

**3. Corresponding Hypothesis Test:** $\displaystyle{\begin{array}{lcl} H_0 & : & \beta_1 = 0\\ H_a & : & \beta_1 \neq 0\end{array}}$

**4. Construct the Model:** We'll use the `{tidymodels}` framework to construct the model. It happens in four steps...(i) `specification`, (ii) `recipe`, (iii) `workflow`, and (iv) `fit`. 

**5. Assess the Model Quality:** Assess the quality of the overall model and individual model terms.

:::{.fragment}

**6. Interpret the Model:** If model quality is sufficient, interpret the resulting model as it pertains to your initial hypothesis.

:::

## `{tidymodels}` Summary for Statistical Learning

<div style="font-size:16pt">

:::{.fragment}

We'll use the `{tidymodels}` framework for constructing our models in MAT300. 

:::

:::{.fragment}

This framework just determines how we'll approach model construction, assessment, and utilization through code.

:::

:::{.fragment}

All of the code we'll need to get started in the ***statistical learning*** setting is summarized below:

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

#Model Construction
model_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

model_rec <- recipe(outcome ~ explanatory_1 + explanatory_2 + ... + explanatory_k, data = my_data)

model_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(model_spec) |>
  add_recipe(model_rec)

model_fit <- model_wf |>
  fit(my_data)

#Model Quality Assessment
model_fit |>
  glance()

model_fit |>
  tidy()
```

:::

</div>

## Machine Learning

<div style="font-size:18pt">

:::{.fragment}

In our *machine learning* context, we seek to identify a best-possible predictive model.

:::

:::{.fragment}

**The Objective:** Given information about an EMS call, predict the response time as accurately as possible.

:::

:::{.fragment}

**1. Define the Outcome Variable:** Total response time, in minutes.

:::

:::{.fragment}

**2. Define the Performance Measure:** We'll need to define how *accuracy* will be measured. There are [many options for regression scenarios](https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/reference/index.html#regression-metrics) -- root mean squared error, mean absolute error, and r-squared are metrics we'll work with in MAT300.

:::

:::{.fragment}

Here, we'll use root mean squared error (RMSE):

:::

:::{.fragment}

$$\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{\left(y_{\text{actual}} - y_{\text{predicted}}\right)^2}}{n}}$$

:::

</div>

## Machine Learning

<div style="font-size:18pt">

**The Objective:** Given information about an EMS call, predict the response time as accurately as possible.

**1. Define the Outcome Variable:** Total response time, in minutes.

**2. Define the Performance Measure:** $\displaystyle{\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{\left(y_{\text{actual}} - y_{\text{predicted}}\right)^2}}{n}}}$

:::{.fragment}

**3. Split Data:** We'll need data to *train* our models on and separate data set(s) to assess them on.

:::

:::{.fragment}

For now, we'll obtain a `train`ing set, a `validation` set, and a final `test`ing set.

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|1|3|5-7|5|6|7|"

set.seed(300)

data_splits <- initial_validation_split(ems, prop = c(0.8, 0.15))

train <- training(data_splits)
validation <- validation(data_splits)
test <- testing(data_splits)
```

:::

</div>

## Machine Learning

<div style="font-size:18pt">

**The Objective:** Given information about an EMS call, predict the response time as accurately as possible.

**1. Define the Outcome Variable:** Total response time, in minutes.

**2. Define the Performance Measure:** $\displaystyle{\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{\left(y_{\text{actual}} - y_{\text{predicted}}\right)^2}}{n}}}$

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="15%"}

**3. Split Data:** 

:::

:::{.column width="85%"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

set.seed(300)

data_splits <- initial_validation_split(ems, prop = c(0.8, 0.15))

train <- training(data_splits)
validation <- validation(data_splits)
test <- testing(data_splits)
```

:::

::::

:::{.fragment}

**4. Conduct EDA on Training Data:** (Omitted here, for time)

:::

:::{.fragment}

**5. Build Models:** Use the same `{tidymodels}` framework as we saw earlier, but be sure to only use the `train`ing data!

:::

</div>

## Machine Learning

<div style="font-size:18pt">

**The Objective:** Given information about an EMS call, predict the response time as accurately as possible.

**1. Define the Outcome Variable:** Total response time, in minutes.

**2. Define the Performance Measure:** $\displaystyle{\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{\left(y_{\text{actual}} - y_{\text{predicted}}\right)^2}}{n}}}$

**3. Split Data:** Obtain training data and validation set(s).

**4. Conduct EDA on Training Data:** (Omitted here, for time)

**5. Build Models:** Use the same `{tidymodels}` framework as we saw earlier, but be sure to only use the `train`ing data!

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-2|4|6-8|10-11|"

lr_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

lr_rec <- recipe(response_time_min ~ distance_mi + traffic_index, data = train)

lr_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lr_spec) |>
  add_recipe(lr_rec)

lr_fit <- lr_wf |>
  fit(train)
```

:::

</div>

## Machine Learning

<div style="font-size:18pt">

**The Objective:** Given information about an EMS call, predict the response time as accurately as possible.

**1. Define the Outcome Variable:** Total response time, in minutes.

**2. Define the Performance Measure:** $\displaystyle{\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{\left(y_{\text{actual}} - y_{\text{predicted}}\right)^2}}{n}}}$

**3. Split Data:** Obtain training data and validation set(s).

**4. Conduct EDA on Training Data:** (Omitted here, for time)

**5. Build Models:** Use the same `{tidymodels}` framework as we saw earlier, but be sure to only use the `train`ing data!

:::{.fragment}

**6. Assess Model Performance:** Measure how well our model performs with respect to our performance metric using in sample (`train`ing) and out of sample (`validation`) data.

:::

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

<center> **Training**</center>

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  augment(train) |>
  rmse(response_time_min, .pred)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  augment(train) |>
  rmse(response_time_min, .pred) |>
  kable()
```

:::

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.fragment}

<center> **Validation**</center>

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_fit |>
  augment(validation) |>
  rmse(response_time_min, .pred)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

lr_fit |>
  augment(validation) |>
  rmse(response_time_min, .pred) |>
  kable()
```

:::

:::

::::

</div>

## Machine Learning

<div style="font-size:18pt">

**The Objective:** Given information about an EMS call, predict the response time as accurately as possible.

**1. Define the Outcome Variable:** Total response time, in minutes.

**2. Define the Performance Measure:** $\displaystyle{\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n}{\left(y_{\text{actual}} - y_{\text{predicted}}\right)^2}}{n}}}$

**3. Split Data:** Obtain training data and validation set(s).

**4. Conduct EDA on Training Data:** (Omitted here, for time)

**5. Build Models:** Use the same `{tidymodels}` framework as we saw earlier, but be sure to only use the `train`ing data!

**6. Assess Model Performance:** Measure how well our model performs with respect to our performance metric using in sample (`train`ing) and out of sample (`validation`) data.

:::{.fragment}

**7. Iterate:** Now you have a benchmark out of sample (`validation`) performance metric. Iterate by constructing new models and trying to improve your metric. Your best performing model always becomes your next benchmark.

:::

</div>

## `{tidymodels}` Summary for Machine Learning

<div style="font-size:16pt">

:::{.fragment}

All of the code we'll need to get started in the ***machine learning*** setting is summarized below:

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

#Split Data
set.seed(300)
data_splits <- initial_validation_split(my_data, prop = c(0.8, 0.15))
train <- training(data_splits)
validation <- validation(data_splits)
test <- testing(data_splits)

#Model Construction
model_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

model_rec <- recipe(outcome ~ explanatory_1 + explanatory_2 + ... + explanatory_k, data = train)

model_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(model_spec) |>
  add_recipe(model_rec)

model_fit <- model_wf |>
  fit(train)

#Model Performance Assessment
model_fit |>
  augment(validation) |>
  rmse(outcome, .pred)
```

:::

</div>

## Wrap-Up Summary

<div style="font-size:17pt">

:::{.fragment}

We still have much more work to do in order to learn how regression works and what our models actually tell us.

:::

:::{.fragment}

Today, we learned a little bit more about the differences (and the similarities) between the ***statistical learning*** and ***machine learning*** settings that we'll encounter in MAT300.

:::

:::{.fragment}

Because we're learning from our data in the ***machine learning*** setting, we need to split our data into subsets that we can *learn* from and then separate sets that we can *validate* and *test* on, to reduce the likelihood that we're just interpreting "noise" in the data.

:::

:::{.fragment}

We don't do this in the ***statistical learning*** setting because we've already come to the modeling project with hypotheses we'd like to test, prior to looking at the data.

:::

:::{.fragment}

The *model construction* code in the `{tidymodels}` framework is the same in both settings.

:::

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

lr_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

lr_rec <- recipe(outcome ~ explanatory_1 + explanatory_2 + ... + explanatory_k, data = my_data_or_train)

lr_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_model(lr_spec) |>
  add_recipe(lr_rec)

lr_fit <- lr_wf |>
  fit(my_data_or_train)
```

:::

</div>
